props.title: The Score
props.initialSlug: The ultimate heist. One last score.

sections.content: The Score stands as one of the last great traditional heist films before digital technology transformed the genre. Robert De Niro and Edward Norton's electric chemistry drives this Montreal-set thriller, with Marlon Brando's final film performance adding gravitas. It follows the classic heist formula established by Rififi (1955) and perfected in The Taking of Pelham One Two Three (1974) - meticulous planning, unexpected complications, and mounting tension. Director Frank Oz trades flashy techniques for methodical precision, mirroring De Niro's careful safecracker.

sections.content: The film's focus on old-school safecracking technique represents a fascinating endpoint for analog heist films. Later entries like Ocean's Eleven (2001) and The Italian Job (2003) would embrace computer hacking and high-tech solutions. The Score deliberately echoes earlier classics like The Asphalt Jungle (1950) and The Anderson Tapes (1971), where success depends on manual skill and nerve rather than digital wizardry.

What sets The Score apart is its exploration of mentorship and betrayal through three generations of actors. Brando's fence represents the old guard, De Niro embodies the consummate professional, and Norton portrays the ambitious new blood. This dynamic recalls The Sting (1973) but with darker undertones about loyalty in the criminal world. The Montreal setting provides a refreshing change from typical American heist locations while adding atmospheric French Canadian flavor. SUBHEAD: The Evolution of Heist Films Post-2001

sections.content: After The Score, heist films increasingly emphasized technology over tradecraft. Swordfish (2001) and Firewall (2006) replaced lockpicks with keyboards. Even traditional heist elements in films like Fast Five (2011) became more about digital manipulation than physical skills. This makes The Score particularly valuable as a bridge between eras, acknowledging changing times while celebrating classic techniques.
